newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew prepares to retrieve satellite.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew prepares to retrieve satellite.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Columbia prepared on Monday to pluck a prototype space factory from orbit, carefully using the orbiter's thrusters to take position for the complicated rendezvous.

Retrieval of the Wake Shield Facility had been moved up by about three hours from the original schedule, so the Orfeus-Spas telescope, an orbiting observatory also deployed by Columbia, would not stray too close to it, NASA officials said.
"We're looking forward to a good rendezvous today," mission control's Bill McArthur said.
NASA had never before flown the shuttle in formation with two recoverable satellites. Flight director Al Pennington said before the mission the task would be "tricky."

When the astronauts woke up they were 23 miles (36.8 km) ahead of the Wake Shield, the experimental factory released by Columbia on Friday night. The orbiter and the satellite moved closer together during the day as they circled far from Earth.
Shuttle commander Ken Cockrell fired Columbia's manoeuvring jets at 3:45 p.m. EST (2045 GMT), positioning the spacecraft for the retrieval, scheduled for 8:56 p.m. EST (0056 GMT on Tuesday).

A second firing of Columbia's manoeuvring jets, called a burn, took place at 6:46 p.m. EST (2345 GMT) and steered the spacecraft toward its final rendezvous with the Wake Shield. The nine-second burn put the orbiter directly on course for the satellite.
"Columbia's new course now can be seen, right on track toward Wake Shield," NASA commentator James Hartsfield said.

Blaring out the pop song "Let the Good Times Roll" by the Cars, mission control had awakened the five astronauts one hour earlier than scheduled so they could begin steering the spacecraft for the interception.

Flight officials at Johnson Space Centre in Houston congratulated astronaut Story Musgrave, 61, on exceeding 1,000 hours in space. Musgrave, the oldest person to fly in space, was making his sixth, and probably last, shuttle flight.
"Story is looking marvellous for a 1,001-hour space traveller," Cockrell, 46, said.
"We just made a beautiful pass over Hawaii. The islands are clear today. No matter how many hours you've got up here, these ones are just as good as the first ones," Musgrave said.
Later on Monday, the astronauts activated the shuttle's 50-foot (17-meter) robot arm, which will be used to grab the Wake Shield.

The space factory and telescope were expected to be 13 miles (21 km) apart when the Columbia swooped in for the retrieval. The craft must be separated by at least 12.5 miles (20 km) for a safe operation, shuttle flight director Rob Kelso said.
The telescope had ceased observations on Sunday so it could be turned to reduce the atmosphere's braking effect on it.

NASA believes the two craft drew unexpectedly close when the Orfeus-Spas telescope encountered more drag than expected from the thin atmosphere 220 miles (355 km) up as it was pointed at its celestial targets. The telescope resumed its activities at about 5 a.m. EST (1000 GMT) on Monday.
The saucer-shaped Wake Shield was designed to manufacture ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry. They could lead to faster computer chips and better, smaller cellular phones.
NASA officials said they were very pleased with the performance of the space factory during the three days it spent orbiting apart from Columbia.
